content: Damek Davis and I have launched a distillation challenge, hosted by the SAIR foundation, to try to distill the ETP implication graph into a short cheat sheet: https://competition.sair.foundation/competitions/mathematics-distillation-challenge-equational-theories-stage1/overview . See also my blog post describing the competition: https://terrytao.wordpress.com/2026/03/13/mathematics-distillation-challenge-equational-theories/

10 kb seems ample space to implement some of the heuristic methods we used to deduce counter examples. If we allow calling external commands then it might also be possible to call external solvers like Knuth-bendix completion tools.
I am guessing there is a more concrete definition of a good solution here,namely, the solution must provide mathematical insights, without resorting to calling external tools.
The easiest cheat sheet for an LLM is to look up our database. So the test equations must come from beyond the ETP
The models we will test the cheatsheets on will have no access to tools or the internet.

The distillation challenge is going surprisingly well so far, with the data sets of test problems we provided now essentially saturated by well-chosen cheat sheets running on open source models. See https://zulip.sair.foundation/#narrow/channel/13-Math-Distillation-Challenge---equational-theories .

One thing that would be interesting would be to supply some additional interesting test data sets outside of the original 22 million ETP set, i.e., implications involving equations of order greater than 4, to see to what extent the current "cheat sheets" generalize outside of the ETP set. Are there any ETP participants that would have for some reason generated such test data sets? Or maybe they possess a list of open implications that one could try the existing cheat sheets on to get an empirical prediction as to their truth value?
Isn't the 677 vs 255 pair still open for finite models? Apologies. It would still count as "in" the dataset

For now we are working with the infinite model graph, which only differs from the finite model graph on about 830 edges, or about 0.03% of the graph, so there may not be enough variation to meaningfully make for a different challenge (unless we heavily overweight the few edges that are different).

This has some data on order 5 implications to Eq2. There are formalized proofs in the linked git branch and some scripts to generate data, but it's been long enough that I don't recall how it all works now. Generally speaking I'd expect just testing the counterexamples from the repo to check for negatives + running vampire to give a quick verification of most order 5 implication pairs.

https://github.com/vlad902/equational_theories/blob/9e6d89011a24dd9a220874754194167d1c9340d0/equational_theories/Generated/Order5/MiscImplications.lean also has some implications not to equation 2 (commit message says it was to establish equivalence classes for some equations, I don't recall now why/which)
